rv.q: A good show may be lurking here, but right now it's all too frantic and disjointed — not so different, if you think about it, from what went on at Studio 54.
In This Ain’t No Disco, the cartoons are infinitely more compelling than the real people.
This Ain't No Disco seriously flounders in its world premiere at off-Broadway's Atlantic Theater.
But mostly “This Ain’t No Disco” just ain’t no fun.

“Tresnjak’s production adds to the sense of fiasco with Brown’s busy but formless choreography and Sherwood’s you-are-nowhere set which at one point wobbles scarily when someone dances on it, providing the show’s single moment of genuine suspense.
The rest of this new musical is just as dumb as that dopey lyric.
The alternately wistful, thoughtful and passionate score, with the emphasis on disco anthems, carries the show along at a breakneck pace.
But if This Ain’t No Disco is never dull, and even intermittently thrilling, it still leaves opportunities not fully realized.
But the glitter here is all just dust.
The score by Stephen Trask and Peter Yanowitz is hard-charging and often melodic, but it isn’t convincing as disco music, if that’s what it’s supposed to be.
What this blue-chip creative team has come up with, however, is surprisingly stolid; a little of the old divine decadence might have pepped things up a bit.
It's impossible to get to know or care about anyone and Darko Tresnjak's relentless production is a visual and aural assault course.
This tiresome show confirms how a poor storyline can scuttle even the brightest of musical talents.
After two hours and 30 minutes of This Ain't No Disco, no lyric has felt truer.
Unfortunately, there's not much else in it either, leaving audiences scratching their heads or scurrying for the exits after watching what can only be described as a hot mess of a musical.
If the performances were not so tight, the music and lyrics of Trask and Yanowitz not so infectious, we might not be so entertained because we know how this story goes and exactly how it ends.
Too often, the show has as little focus as a broken Instamatic.
As a chorus of “supplicants” clamors to be let in, it's tempting to confess they're not missing much.
The result, then, is rather pointless and dull, stuffed with forgettable tunes and anchored by a boilerplate Star Is Born narrative.

"Some of 'This Ain't No Disco's' tunes are catchy but the overall score lacks cohesion...Their narrative totally fails to deliver. Its dialog, delivered in rhyming couplets, isn't nearly as clever as it wants to be.
The result is a shallow, disconnected, and unsuccessful mish-mash, with no believable characterizations, no incisive humor, and no authentic evocation of the period.
This isn’t just a flop, but a belly flop—the likes of which you rarely see on stage in New York anymore.

Key parts of that history course through the combination of facts and fiction making up This Ain’t No Disco, a disappointing rock musical at the Atlantic, its title drawn from a lyric in the Talking Heads song, “Life during Wartime.”

cn.t: Critics find this Studio 54-set rock opera a confusing, cliché-filled "hot mess" that fails to capture the era's excitement. Despite energetic performances and strong music, the muddled storytelling and insubstantial characters leave most reviewers cold.
